Niche breadth indices from pairwise isodar parameters

Source: R/pairwise_niche.R
pairwise_niche.Rd

Summarises the intercepts and slopes of the pairwise isodars directly (Appendix S1 of Granot, Dubiner & Belmaker), as an alternative to the isodar-adjusted inequality (iai()), and checks that the isodars are consistent with each other. A perfect generalist has intercepts of 0 and slopes of 1 between all habitat pairs.

Usage

pairwise_niche(
  isodars,
  weights = NULL,
  scale = c("log", "linear"),
  cycle_tolerance = log(1.5),
  log_slope = NULL
)

Arguments

isodars

Pairwise isodars from fit_isodars(dim = "pairwise"), or a data frame with columns habitat_x, habitat_y, intercept, slope (and sd, the SD of perpendicular residuals, for weights = "1/var").

weights

NULL (equal weights), "1/var" (inverse variance of each isodar; see Details), or a numeric vector with one non-negative weight per isodar.

scale

"log" (default; orientation-invariant indices) or "linear" (the earlier indices); see Details.

cycle_tolerance

Largest acceptable \(|\log(product)|\) of slopes around a cycle of three habitats (default log(1.5)).

log_slope

Deprecated: use scale. TRUE is scale = "log" and FALSE is scale = "linear".

Value

An object of class pairwise_niche, a list with

  • indices: a one-row tibble. For scale = "log": mean_abs_log_slope, mean_distance, slope_niche_breadth, intercept_niche_breadth, n_isodars, n_slope (isodars used for the slope indices) and note. For scale = "linear": mean_intercept, mean_slope, slope_niche_breadth, intercept_niche_breadth, n_isodars and note.

  • cycles: a tibble with one row per cycle of three habitats with isodars between all three pairs: habitat_1, habitat_2, habitat_3, product (\(b_{12} b_{23} b_{31}\)), log_product and inconsistent.

  • inconsistent: TRUE if any cycle is inconsistent.

  • isodars: the isodars used, with their weight, and for scale = "log" the distance \(d\) and log_slope; for scale = "linear" they are oriented to non-negative intercepts.

  • scale, cycle_tolerance.

Details

Orientation invariance. An isodar between habitats \(i\) and \(j\) can be written with either habitat on the x-axis: \(N_j = a + b N_i\) or, equivalently, \(N_i = -a/b + (1/b) N_j\). With scale = "log" (default) every index is the same whichever way each isodar is written:

  • slope deviations are \((\log b)^2\), since \(\log(1/b) = -\log b\);

  • intercept deviations use the perpendicular distance of the isodar from the origin, \(d = |a| / \sqrt{1 + b^2}\), which is the same for both ways of writing the line.

The variance-based indices are $$1 / \sqrt{\sum w (\log b)^2 / \sum w}$$ for slopes and $$1 / \sqrt{\sum w d^2 / \sum w}$$ for intercepts, where \(w\) are the isodar weights. They measure deviations from the values that indicate no habitat preference (\(b = 1\), \(d = 0\)). Larger values indicate broader niches; extreme specialists approach 0, and a perfect generalist gives Inf. The mean indices are the weighted means of \(|\log b|\) and of \(d\).

With weights = "1/var" and scale = "log", each isodar is weighted by \(1/sd^2\), the inverse variance of its perpendicular residuals, which is also orientation-invariant.

Non-positive slopes (for example, a habitat that loses individuals as another gains them) have no logarithm. Such isodars are left out of the slope indices, with a warning naming them, but still used in the intercept indices.

Linear scale. scale = "linear" gives the earlier indices: each isodar is first expressed so that its intercept is non-negative (habitats swapped if needed), then the mean intercept and mean slope, and \(1 / \sqrt{\sum w (b - 1)^2 / \sum w}\) and \(1 / \sqrt{\sum w a^2 / \sum w}\), with "1/var" weights \(1/(sd^2(1+b^2))\). These depend on how each isodar is oriented, and slopes of 2 and 0.5 (preferences of equal strength in opposite directions) count as different deviations.

Consistency check. If the isodars describe one consistent pattern of habitat selection, the slopes around any cycle of three habitats multiply to 1: \(b_{AB} b_{BC} b_{CA} = 1\), where \(b_{AB}\) is the slope of habitat \(B\) on habitat \(A\). Each cycle's product is returned in cycles, and the result is flagged as inconsistent when \(|\log(product)|\) exceeds cycle_tolerance for any cycle (or the product is not positive).

Units. The intercept indices are in units of abundance per sampling unit (see reference_effort in fit_isodars()), so they depend on survey effort and are comparable among species only when surveys are standardised. The slope indices are unitless.

See also

fit_isodars(), iai()

Examples

set.seed(1)
sim <- simulate_isodars(1.5, 1.5, 5, 5, noise = 1, n = 30)
pw <- fit_isodars(sim, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3"))
pn <- pairwise_niche(pw, weights = "1/var")
pn
#> Niche breadth from pairwise isodars (log scale)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 7
#>   mean_abs_log_slope mean_distance slope_niche_breadth intercept_niche_breadth
#>                <dbl>         <dbl>               <dbl>                   <dbl>
#> 1              0.486          3.37                1.95                   0.285
#> # ℹ 3 more variables: n_isodars <int>, n_slope <int>, note <chr>
#> 1 cycle(s) of three habitats; 0 inconsistent (|log(product of slopes)| > 0.405); see $cycles
pn$cycles
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   habitat_1 habitat_2 habitat_3 product log_product inconsistent
#>   <chr>     <chr>     <chr>       <dbl>       <dbl> <lgl>       
#> 1 hab1      hab2      hab3        0.999   -0.000649 FALSE       
pairwise_niche(pw, scale = "linear")$indices
#> # A tibble: 1 × 6
#>   mean_intercept mean_slope slope_niche_breadth intercept_niche_brea…¹ n_isodars
#>            <dbl>      <dbl>               <dbl>                  <dbl>     <int>
#> 1           7.79       1.75                1.21                  0.116         3
#> # ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​intercept_niche_breadth
